content: A centrifugal pump may develop abnormal vibration because of imbalance, misalignment, bearing deterioration, cavitation, looseness, hydraulic instability, or foundation issues. Investigation should compare current vibration trends with historical baseline, operating conditions, maintenance history, and inspection findings. The AI system should distinguish measured observations from hypotheses and should not declare a root cause without sufficient evidence.

Preventive maintenance uses scheduled inspection, lubrication, alignment checks, vibration monitoring, thermography, and component condition checks to reduce unexpected equipment failures. Maintenance intervals should be determined from approved plant procedures, equipment manuals, condition-monitoring history, and site-specific reliability programs.

Common refinery rotating equipment includes pumps, compressors, turbines, blowers, and fans. Typical engineering checks include vibration, temperature, lubrication condition, shaft alignment, coupling condition, seal performance, bearing condition, and operating load. Actual equipment limits must be taken from the approved equipment datasheet or manufacturer documentation.

Instrumentation systems may include pressure, temperature, flow, level, vibration, and analytical measurements. Troubleshooting should consider sensor health, calibration status, signal quality, wiring, transmitters, control valves, PLC/DCS configuration, and process conditions. A suspicious reading should be cross-checked against redundant measurements or independent process indicators when available.

Process troubleshooting should begin with the observed deviation, relevant operating parameters, recent changes, equipment status, alarms, and historical trends. Possible explanations should be treated as hypotheses until supported by evidence. Process engineers should use approved operating envelopes and unit-specific procedures when determining whether a condition is abnormal.

When an important process alarm occurs, the operator should acknowledge and assess the alarm according to the approved operating procedure, verify related process indications, check recent trends and interacting alarms, and take only authorized actions. Emergency or abnormal-operation procedures take precedence over generic guidance.

Refinery safety management includes hazard identification, permit-to-work controls, isolation and lockout/tagout, gas testing, personal protective equipment, emergency response, incident investigation, and management of change. Site-specific safety procedures and legal requirements must take precedence over generic information.

Corrosion assessment may use inspection history, thickness measurements, corrosion-rate calculations, visual inspection, non-destructive examination, process chemistry, and operating conditions. A corrosion trend should be evaluated using multiple inspection points and appropriate time intervals rather than a single measurement.

Equipment condition assessment can include visual examination and non-destructive testing such as ultrasonic thickness measurement, radiography, magnetic particle testing, dye penetrant testing, or other approved methods. Inspection acceptance criteria must come from the applicable engineering standard, inspection plan, or approved site procedure.

A structured failure investigation should record the asset, failure symptom, date and time, operating state, alarms, maintenance history, inspection observations, recent interventions, and available sensor trends. Candidate causes should be compared against evidence. The final conclusion should identify verified facts, supported inferences, unresolved questions, and recommended evidence collection.

An increase in bearing temperature can be associated with lubrication problems, excessive load, misalignment, bearing degradation, cooling problems, or environmental effects. Temperature alone does not establish a root cause. Trend behavior, load, lubrication records, vibration data, and maintenance history should be considered together.

Potential indications of pump cavitation can include abnormal noise, fluctuating discharge pressure, unstable flow, vibration changes, and degraded hydraulic performance. These indicators can have other causes, so confirmation should consider suction conditions, fluid properties, operating point, and approved pump performance information.

Condition-monitoring analytics should compare current measurements with historical behavior and relevant operating context. Useful features may include rolling averages, rate of change, deviation from baseline, alarm frequency, and correlation with operating state. Statistical correlation should not automatically be interpreted as physical causation.

Engineering answers should preserve document identity, revision, date, source classification, and relevant section or page information. Retrieval systems should apply user authorization and document classification filters before placing retrieved content into the AI context.

The AI workbench should present verified findings with evidence references, distinguish observations from inferences, explicitly identify uncertainty or contradictions, and derive confidence from evidence verification rather than model self-rating alone. The system should not silently promote an unsupported hypothesis to a confirmed finding.
